title: Stefanie Braun & Gabriel Lee, "Income and density spillover effects in German land prices," Journal of European Real Estate Research (Emerald), 2026
what_was_fetched: Full text was not obtained. Direct curl with a browser user-agent to the DOI (resolves to emerald.com) returned HTTP 403; r.jina.ai returned Emerald's Cloudflare 'performing security verification' challenge page; a Googlebot user-agent also returned 403 on both the DOI and the Crossref-listed direct PDF URL (emerald.com/jerer/article-pdf/.../jerer-11-2025-0095en.pdf), and r.jina.ai on that same PDF URL hit the same Cloudflare challenge. This 2021 working paper is almost certainly an earlier draft/precursor of the same research programme (same 2014-2018 county-level residential land-price data, same core income/density agglomeration question) but is NOT the JERER 2026 paper: its reported point estimates differ substantially (1% income -> 3.45% land-price increase; 1% density -> 5.47%, with no direct/indirect split reported) from the published version's abstract (see below), so it should be treated as background context on the research trajectory, not substituted for the actual queue item's findings.
verdict: ENRICH places/germany.md and concepts/agglomeration-economies.md. Per the T0 brief's own guidance (NEW page only if full text was read), this stays an enrichment: add a paragraph to germany.md's overview or a new short subsection citing the county-level Bodenrichtwert-based land-price spillover finding as further evidence of the agglomeration-to-land-rent channel Germany's Grundsteuer/Bodenwertsteuer discussion already sits within, and cross-link from concepts/agglomeration-economies.md's 'Link to Land Values' section, which currently has no German case study. Do not create a dedicated research/ page from an abstract alone.
claim_grade: B-claim (quantitative empirical findings, but abstract-level only -- the SDM regression tables, robustness checks, and exact county sample were not independently examined). Tier: both authors are University of Regensburg real-estate-economics academics (Gabriel Lee holds a professorship and chairs the university's Chair of Real Estate Economics, with a prior peer-reviewed publication record on German land prices including a Journal of Housing Economics-adjacent 2022 paper, 'The prices of residential land in German counties'); this supports treating them as established academics under EDITORIAL SS4c ('established academics with a peer-reviewed body of work on the topic'), i.e. Tier 1, but neither name is yet in sources/audit/people-tiers.json -- T1 should confirm and add them if this stands.
content_summary: Per the Crossref/Semantic Scholar abstract: the paper uses a Spatial Durbin Model (SDM) on German county-level residential and vacant (development-designated) land prices, 2014-2018, to separate DIRECT (own-county) from INDIRECT (spillover-to-neighboring-county) effects of median income and population density. Findings, quoted/paraphrased directly from the abstract: a 1% increase in median income raises local land prices by 1.5-2.5% (direct effect) and neighboring-county land prices by a further 0.5-0.9% (indirect/spillover effect); a 1% increase in population density raises local land prices by 2-3% (direct) and 1.5-2% indirectly. Both effects are more pronounced in suburban counties near large metropolitan areas (the clustering finding referenced in the queue context) and more pronounced for residential land than for vacant/development land, which the authors attribute to realized-use and regulatory constraints amplifying spatial externalities. The paper frames itself as linking the agglomeration-economics and spatial-housing-dynamics literatures to land valuation specifically, and its stated policy upshot is that housing-affordability and regional-price-disparity interventions should account for the spatial diffusion of land-price shocks, not just local supply/demand.
existing_wiki_coverage: places/germany.md (read in full) currently covers Germany's low homeownership/rental-market stability, the Loffler & Siegloch Grundsteuer rent-pass-through study, and the 2025 Baden-Wurttemberg Bodenwertsteuer reform -- all institutional/tax-incidence content, with no existing coverage of the agglomeration/spatial-spillover determinants of German land VALUES themselves. concepts/agglomeration-economies.md (read in full) already covers Duranton & Puga (2023), Kanemoto/Ohkawara/Suzuki's Japan HGT test, Hsieh & Moretti, and Fiorentino & Moogan's LVT-agglomeration model, but has no empirical German case and no direct/indirect spatial-spillover decomposition of the kind this paper supplies -- this would be new, non-duplicative content in both places.
uncertainties: No full text, so the SDM specification's controls, the exact county sample and count, statistical significance levels, and any limitations/robustness section the authors themselves flag are unknown and cannot be represented. The relationship between this paper and the 2021 BGPE working paper's different point estimates (3.45%/5.47% vs. the published 1.5-2.5%/2-3% direct effects) is not explained by anything read this pass -- it may reflect a refined specification, a different sample cut, or the direct/indirect decomposition simply not existing in the 2021 draft; T1 should not merge the two papers' numbers. Whether the Bodenrichtwert (official land-value benchmark) is confirmed as the land-price series used, as the T0 prompt guessed, could not be verified from the abstract alone.

Tier: Maria Alessandra Rossi is Associate Professor of Economic Policy at the University of Chieti-Pescara and Scientific Coordinator of the Centre for a Digital Society at the European University Institute, with a peer-reviewed record in competition/regulation economics -- this supports Tier 1 ('established academics with a peer-reviewed body of work on the topic') under SS4c, though she is not yet in sources/audit/people-tiers.json and T1 should confirm.
content_summary: Per the Crossref/Semantic Scholar abstract (quoted near-verbatim): the survey reviews the macroeconomic market-power literature -- measurement (concentration ratios, business-dynamism indicators, markup/markdown estimates), drivers, and macroeconomic effects -- and documents 'a distinct change in trends since the 1980s, especially in the United States,' characterized by 'stable median markups alongside rising upper-tail dispersion and reallocation toward a small set of high-markup firms,' while noting developments in Europe and elsewhere are 'more heterogeneous and context-dependent.' It frames a central open tension between technology-based explanations (scale economies, automation, intangibles) and competition-based explanations (conduct, entry barriers, regulation), and states that 'the evidence linking market power to declining labor shares, rising profits, and increasing wage dispersion and inequality is strong, while effects on productivity, investment, and innovation are more nuanced and non-monotonic.' It bills itself as providing 'a methodological assessment' that 'reconciles competing interpretations' and draws out 'implications for macroeconomic and competition policy.' No specific numeric findings (e.g. exact markup ratios) appear in the abstract itself -- those would need the full text.

None of these pages currently cite a synthesizing survey; this Rossi paper's abstract-stated 'stable median, rising upper-tail dispersion' framing independently corroborates (from a source the wiki has not yet used) exactly the distributional shape De Loecker/Eeckhout/Unger document, which is a genuine, non-duplicative addition even at abstract level.

The abstract does not mention land, rent, or Georgism in any form, so no claim should be made that the survey engages the wiki's core land-rent thesis -- it should be cited strictly as generalist market-power synthesis evidence, per the wiki's existing pattern for the De Loecker cluster.

title: Jonathan Becker, Corina Boar & Virgiliu Midrigan, "Importers, Market Power and Optimal Tariffs," NBER Working Paper 35829, September 2026
what_was_fetched: Full text was obtained and read in full (66 pages including appendix). Direct curl with a browser user-agent to the NBER PDF URL (nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w35829/w35829.pdf) returned HTTP 403 (an NBER login/paywall interstitial, confirmed by inspecting the returned HTML, which was NOT the actual PDF despite the .pdf extension). r.jina.ai on the same URL succeeded (HTTP 200) and returned the complete 66-page paper as clean text, including the abstract, full model derivations, all tables, and the reference list -- saved at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-georgism-wiki/27113c0d-0e4a-5705-a87d-69e4d8108829/scratchpad/t0-2026-09-28/item3_jina.txt. A full-text grep for 'land', 'Georgis', 'rent', and 'rents' (case-insensitive, whole-word) returned ZERO matches anywhere in the paper -- confirmed directly, not inferred: this paper never uses the word 'rent' in any sense, including the market-power-as-rent sense the wiki's other market-power pages (De Loecker/Eeckhout/Unger, De Loecker/Eeckhout/Mongey, Kaplow) all explicitly invoke.
verdict: ENRICH, narrowly -- not REJECT, but also not a NEW page. Per the T0 prompt's own framing ('default ENRICH... or REJECT as too remote, unless the paper says something specific about rents that a Georgist reader needs'): the paper says nothing about rents in any register, and its subject (optimal tariff design) is one step further from the wiki's core mission than the domestic market-power papers already on the wiki. But it directly extends the same underlying question Kaplow (2019) asks -- does the presence of market-power distortions change standard optimal-policy prescriptions? -- into trade policy, and reaches a genuinely counter-intuitive, well-identified result (negative optimal tariffs, i.e. import SUBSIDIES) that is worth one paragraph on concepts/rent-seeking.md's existing 'Tax-Design Implications' section (which already discusses Kaplow and Rothschild & Scheuer) or research/kaplow-market-power.md's 'Bears On' list, framed explicitly as a market-power/optimal-policy result in a different domain, not as rent-related content.
claim_grade: B-claim (peer-reviewed-caliber NBER working paper, not yet formally peer-reviewed; full text read and all headline figures below verified directly against the primary text, not summarized secondhand). Tier: all three authors (Jonathan Becker, Stony Brook University; Corina Boar, NYU and NBER; Virgiliu Midrigan, NYU and NBER) are established academic economists at research universities with NBER affiliations -- Tier 1 under SS4c, though none is yet in sources/audit/people-tiers.json.
content_summary: The paper models heterogeneous firms that pay a fixed cost to import intermediate inputs (so only the most efficient firms import) and charge markups that rise with firm size (via a Kimball demand aggregator, contrasted throughout against a constant-markup CES benchmark). Motivating facts: only 5.5% of US firms import but they account for nearly half of US employment; importers have 25% higher measured labor productivity; importers pass through only 62% of cost changes to prices (all cited to prior literature, not this paper's own data). Core result: market power means importers are TOO FEW and TOO SMALL relative to the efficient allocation -- the planner would raise the import-firm share from 5.5% to 8.7% and their employment share from 50% to 96%. Eliminating these distortions would raise consumption by 10.1% in the calibrated (Kimball) economy versus only 1.7% in the CES benchmark. A 10% unilateral tariff REDUCES consumption by 0.75% in the Kimball economy (versus RAISING it 0.33% in CES) because it pushes marginal importers to stop importing, cutting aggregate productivity by 2.5% (vs 1% in CES). The paper's headline optimal-tariff results: in the static calibrated economy the optimal tariff is -8.1% (i.e., an import SUBSIDY), against +16.2% in the otherwise-identical CES economy and roughly +30% if the import-selection margin is held fixed; in the richer dynamic economy (elastic labor, capital accumulation, endogenous entry, trade imbalances) the optimal tariff is -12%, against +10.3% for CES. The optimal tariff DECREASES with country/economy size -- -12% when the modeled country is half of world trade, -3.3% at one quarter, +19.9% at 1% of world trade -- because a large country's tariff meaningfully depresses foreign demand for its own exports (the 'repercussion effect'), which weakens the standard terms-of-trade motive for a positive tariff. The paper is explicit that abstracting from either firm selection into importing or variable markups (i.e., using a standard CES trade model) understates the true cost of tariffs and wrongly concludes a positive tariff is optimal.
existing_wiki_coverage: research/kaplow-market-power.md (read in full) is the closest existing analogue: it asks a structurally similar question (does market power change optimal policy design?) for domestic income taxation and finds standard prescriptions survive 'largely intact.' This NBER paper reaches the opposite-flavored conclusion in the trade-policy domain -- market power substantially changes the optimal-tariff prescription, flipping its sign -- which makes an interesting, honest contrast worth one sentence in Kaplow's 'Bears On' section or concepts/rent-seeking.md's 'Tax-Design Implications' section, both of which already juxtapose Kaplow against Rothschild & Scheuer on a similar theme. No existing wiki page covers optimal tariff theory or import/trade market power at all.
uncertainties: None regarding the paper's own content (full text read and headline numbers verified against the primary text). The open editorial question is scope: this is a technical international-trade optimal-policy paper with no rent, land, or Georgist content of any kind, so T1 should weigh honestly whether even a one-sentence mention over-extends the wiki's remit versus genuinely serving the 'does market power change optimal policy' throughline the Kaplow/Rothschild-Scheuer material already establishes. A REJECT verdict would also be defensible; this brief's ENRICH recommendation is a judgment call, not a clear-cut case either way.

title: Seeraj Mohamed, "A Heterodox Developmental Economics Understanding of Systemic Corruption: The Case of South Africa," The Strategic Review for Southern Africa 48(1), 2026
what_was_fetched: Full text was obtained and read in full. The DOI resolved directly (HTTP 200, no block) to the journal's OJS article page (upjournals.up.ac.za, University of Pretoria), which linked to the article's 'view' page, which in turn exposed the direct PDF download URL (upjournals.up.ac.za/index.php/strategic_review/article/download/7468/5332/30730); that PDF (340KB, 9 pages) downloaded cleanly with a browser user-agent and no bot-block at any step, and was extracted to full text with PyMuPDF -- saved at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-georgism-wiki/27113c0d-0e4a-5705-a87d-69e4d8108829/scratchpad/t0-2026-09-28/item4_mohamed.pdf and item4_mohamed.txt. This was the only one of the four queue items where the actual journal-published PDF, not an abstract or a working-paper substitute, was obtained.
verdict: NEW research page (e.g. research/mohamed-heterodox-corruption-south-africa.md) AND enrich both concepts/rent-seeking.md and places/south-africa.md with cross-links to it -- satisfying the README's >=2-inbound-link requirement for a new page. Full text was read; the paper is a substantive, coherent, citable peer-reviewed journal article that directly engages Mushtaq Khan's rent framework (already Tier 1 and load-bearing on concepts/rent-seeking.md) and fills a real content gap on places/south-africa.md, which currently covers only site-value-rating/Katz-Commission history and has no coverage at all of South Africa's post-apartheid corruption, state-capture, or financialisation political economy.
claim_grade: B/C-claim mix: the paper is itself a heterodox-economics SYNTHESIS/argumentative essay (EDITORIAL SS2 type D, interpretive/argumentative) built on secondary literature (Khan, Amsden, Bhorat et al., Fine & Rustomjee, Gabor & Braun) rather than the author's own new empirical dataset, so its central thesis should be presented as 'Mohamed argues...' not as settled fact; the specific cited figures (e.g. the ZAR303.1bn/ZAR244.3bn IPP contingent-liability numbers, sourced by Mohamed to South Africa's own 2026 Budget Review) are A-claims (official government data, secondhand through this source). Tier: Seeraj Mohamed holds a PhD in Economics (University of Massachusetts Amherst), is Deputy Director: Economics at the South African Parliamentary Budget Office (a statutory body of Parliament) and Adjunct Professor at the University of the Western Cape, with a peer-reviewed publication record (International Review of Applied Economics, Development) specifically on South African financialisation and corporate structure -- this supports Tier 1 ('established academics with a peer-reviewed body of work on the topic' / quasi-official body standing) under SS4c, though he is not yet in sources/audit/people-tiers.json and T1 should confirm and add him.
content_summary: Central thesis: developmental states must manage economic rents by disciplining vested interests and directing capital toward productive investment (citing Amsden's South Korea, where Park-era subsidies/tariff protection came with strict reciprocal export-performance conditions); post-apartheid South Africa failed to build such a state, so 'large corporations have retained significant control over the economy while investing relatively little in productive domestic development and continuing to extract wealth,' and 'limited legitimate economic opportunities encouraged... an aspiring elite... to pursue rents through corruption and state capture' -- the paper's core reframe is that corruption/state capture (the Zuma-era 'shadow state' literature, citing Bhorat et al. 2017) should be read as a SYMPTOM of this broader extractive structure, not its primary cause. Directly cites and quotes Mushtaq Khan's rent definition and typology -- 'an income which is higher than the minimum which an individual or firm would have accepted given alternative opportunities' (Khan 2000, 5) and rent-seeking as 'activities which seek to create, maintain or change the rights and institutions on which particular rents are based' (Khan 2000, 6) -- drawn from Khan's edited volume Rents, Rent-Seeking and Economic Development (Cambridge University Press, 2000), which is the SAME primary source the wiki's own concepts/rent-seeking.md Source 15 explicitly flags as 'not yet... consulted' (it currently cites only Khan's 2010 SOAS working paper). Covers: the minerals-energy-finance complex (MEC/MEFC, Fine & Rustomjee) as South Africa's system of accumulation; GEAR (1996) as the pivot to neoliberal macro policy; Eskom's capture and the REI4P renewable-energy IPP program as a 'derisking macro-finance regime' (Gabor & Braun 2023) where the state privately guarantees IPP power-purchase agreements -- National Treasury's 2026 Budget Review reports ZAR303.1 billion in contingent liabilities to independent power producers, with ZAR244.3 billion in exposure. Financialisation is argued to intensify 'speculative and rent-seeking behaviour' via financial liberalisation since the 1990s, drawing on Critical Macro Finance (Gabor 2020) literature.
existing_wiki_coverage: concepts/rent-seeking.md (read in full) already carries a dedicated Mushtaq Khan section ('A Development-Economics Qualification: Not All Rents Are Alike'), sourced to Khan's 2010 SOAS paper and explicitly noting his fuller 2000 Rents, Rent-Seeking and Economic Development volume 'has not yet been consulted.' This Mohamed paper supplies secondhand quoted access to exactly that unconsulted 2000 volume's definitions, which is a genuine, citable lead T1/Hermes should follow up by sourcing Khan (2000) directly if possible. places/south-africa.md (read in full) currently covers only municipal site-value rating history (Transvaal ordinance, 2004 MPRA) and the 1998-99 Katz Commission's land-tax feasibility inquiry -- it has zero existing coverage of state capture, corruption, financialisation, or the MEC/MEFC accumulation-system literature, all of which this paper would add as a wholly new section.
uncertainties: The paper is a secondary-literature synthesis/argument piece, not primary quantitative research of its own -- a wiki page must attribute its central claims to Mohamed's argument (and the authors he draws on, especially his own prior co-authored Khan & Mohamed 2023) rather than presenting them as independently-established empirical fact, per EDITORIAL SS2's Type D (interpretive/argumentative) sourcing rule. The paper is explicitly framed around South Africa's own political-economy specifics and does not address land value taxation, LVT, or the Katz Commission material already on places/south-africa.md at all, so the new content is additive/parallel rather than in dialogue with the wiki's existing South Africa coverage -- a T1 editor should decide whether to keep these as separate sections or explicitly bridge them (e.g., noting the tension between the extractive-rent argument here and the land-rent-capture argument in the existing Katz Commission section).
